extraction.reason: Not recorded when the page was cached, and not recovered since. What the .txt shows is a tag-stripping of the .html rather than a browser rendering: it keeps the site navigation chrome, decodes entities, holds each paragraph on one line, and carries artefacts only a regex stripper leaves - a bare `--->` where a comment opened with a `>` inside it, and a fragment of a meta attribute ending `">`. Two candidates were run on 2026-09-09 and NEITHER reproduces extractedTextSha256: a regex stripper (tags to newlines, entities decoded, blank lines dropped) and Chromium's document.body.innerText through Playwright. This is not cosmetic: content/levels/prairie-rail.json cites this digest as the sourceHash of its territory statement, so a shipped claim is pinned to bytes that only a machine already holding the file can produce. Someone who fetched the page and matched its sha256 still cannot check the quote.

knownStaleness.topic: A scholarly account, not a nation's own
knownStaleness.problem: This entry is a university encyclopedia article. It is a citable source for WHEN and WHERE Treaty 4 was made and for the extent of the land it covers, and it is not a nation speaking for itself. It writes the two treaty parties as `Cree and Saulteaux`, which is the wording content/levels/prairie-rail.json carries into `nations`; the level's nationSource is the File Hills Qu'Appelle Tribal Council, eleven Treaty Four First Nations whose own names include Peepeekisis Cree Nation, Star Blanket Cree Nation and Muscowpetung Saulteaux Nation, which is what makes those two spellings names those nations use rather than an author's choice.
knownStaleness.action: prefer a Treaty Four institution's own account if one becomes reachable; this entry was cached because the Parks Canada prairie sites carry no territorial statement and treaty4.ca did not resolve on 9 September 2026

knownStaleness.topic: Nineteenth-century terms quoted inside the article
knownStaleness.problem: The article quotes 1874 correspondence that uses `Indians` and `tribes`, and it reproduces the Crown's framing of the treaty as a cession. Nothing quoted into a level document may carry that language to a player.
knownStaleness.action: quote only the article's own sentences, never the correspondence it reproduces, and paraphrase into plain language before it reaches a screen

grainNote: One article, one heading. Both flags are at chapter grain because there is nothing finer to point at, and both are about the SOURCE rather than about drift: neither clears by re-fetching.

claimsCompared: the extent of the treaty area: "The treaty ceded 195,000 square km of territory ranging from the southeast corner of present-day Alberta through most of southern Saskatchewan to west-central Manitoba."
the date and place of the negotiations: the commissioners were sent "to Fort Qu'Appelle on September 8, 1874, to conduct negotiations on behalf of the British Crown"
the two parties as the article itself writes them: "the strategy of the Cree and Saulteaux was to gain full compensation for their lands"
the article's framing of the treaty as a cession, which the second staleness flag covers
the nineteenth-century correspondence the article reproduces, including Indian Agent Allan Macdonald's "this site ... represents the place on which the Treaty was signed"
the absence of any modification or review date anywhere on the page
